findings.headline: AI governance framework not yet in place despite staff using external tools without approval
findings.detail: New Very High risk (14/15) added to register. Controls are noted as 'in development'. The council reports staff independently using public AI platforms (ChatGPT etc.) without approval, risking entry of personal and commercially sensitive council data into external systems. The council lacks clarity on data ownership and reuse by AI providers. Actions include development of a council-wide AI governance framework.
findings.matters: Data breaches from unsanctioned external AI tool use could create legal liability and regulatory intervention; governance lag on a rapidly-emerging risk creates operational and reputational exposure
findings.figures: Very High risk rating 14 (Impact 3 × Likelihood 4)
findings.quote: Staff independently using publicly available AI platforms (eg generative AI tools) without approval

findings.headline: HRA faces very high financial pressure from rising demand and new building standards
findings.detail: The council identifies a Very High risk (14/15) to housing revenue account viability. Demand for accommodation exceeds availability due to socioeconomic factors. Stock condition does not meet regulatory standards. New requirements like Awaabs Law and revised decent homes standards create additional pressure. The council reports insufficient financial and staffing resources to address these needs.
findings.matters: The HRA is a core revenue stream and borrowing vehicle for councils; pressure here signals funding stress that could constrain capital capacity or affect council creditworthiness
findings.figures: Very High risk rating 14 (Impact 3 × Likelihood 4)
findings.quote: Insufficient resources available – financial, people (capacity and knowledge) to allocate to addressing needs as well as new housing requirements/regulations eg Awaabs Law, new decent homes standard etc

findings.paper_title: Appendix A for Treasury Management Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Financing cost ratios diverged materially from budget
findings.detail: Non-HRA financing costs ratio was (8.59%) actual compared to (4.12%) budgeted, a 4.5 percentage point variance. HRA went from 1.07% budgeted to (2.35%) actual, a 3.4 point swing. These material variances indicate treasury performance or assumptions diverged significantly from forecast.
findings.matters: Significant treasury variances affect forecast accuracy and cash flow planning; the finance director would need to understand what drove such large divergences.
findings.figures: Non-HRA variance 4.47pp (budget 4.12%, actual 8.59%); HRA variance 3.42pp (budget 1.07%, actual 2.35%)
findings.quote: Ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream     Non-HRA (8.29%) (4.12%) (8.59%)

findings.paper_title: Appendix A for Treasury Management Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Non-HRA capital expenditure overran budget by £1.4m (9%)
findings.detail: Non-HRA capital spending was £16.565m against a budget of £15.179m, a 9% overspend. Total capital expenditure was £37.549m versus budget of £36.270m. The capital programme exceeded plan, which could indicate delivery challenges or scope changes.
findings.matters: Capital overruns signal execution risk and forecast accuracy issues, affecting the council's ability to deliver planned investment without additional borrowing.
findings.figures: Non-HRA actual £16.565m vs budget £15.179m (£1.386m overspend); total actual £37.549m vs budget £36.270m

findings.headline: Housing revenue account required reserve drawdown for unbudgeted in-year spending pressures
findings.detail: The council drew on HRA reserves during 2025/26 to cover in-year spending pressures, indicating the budget did not fully provide for actual costs. This is a direct and stated reason for the decline in overall liquid reserves available for investment.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted HRA spending pressures suggest either inadequate budgeting or emerging cost pressures in a major service area, both material to council financial management and sustainability
findings.figures: HRA reserve drawdown contributed to overall investment portfolio reduction of approximately £15.2m
findings.quote: This follows on from the outturn position where there was a need to draw on the HRA reserves to fund in-year spending pressures, internal borrowing for Depot project and use of reserves to fund capital expenditure.

findings.headline: Investment portfolio declined sharply as reserves were drawn to fund capital programme and HRA pressures
findings.detail: South Kesteven's investment portfolio fell to an average of £51.260m in Q1 2026/27 from £66.479m in the same period last year. The council drew on reserves during 2025/26 to fund capital expenditure and meet in-year spending pressures in the housing revenue account, directly causing a £415k shortfall against the budgeted investment income of £2.479m.
findings.matters: Declining liquidity and reliance on reserve drawdown to cover expenses budgeted in normal operations weakens the council's financial resilience and raises questions about sustainability
findings.figures: Portfolio average £51.260m vs £66.479m prior year; £415k investment income shortfall against budget of £2.479m
findings.quote: The reduction in the portfolio is largely due to use of reserves to fund the capital programme during the 2025/26 financial year alongside internal borrowing for the depot project in order to avoid incurring external borrowing costs.

findings.committee: Finance and Economic Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Appendix B for Housing Revenue Account Provisional Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Cabinet approved rent convergence from April 2027 with increases of CPI+1% plus annual cash uplift
findings.detail: Cabinet has approved rent convergence policy that will increase HRA rents by CPI+1%+£1 for 2027/28 and CPI+1%+£2 from 2028/29. Modeling is currently underway to assess the additional income impact to be incorporated into the business plan.
findings.matters: Material change to income assumptions; lenders need to understand the council's planned income trajectory and whether rent policy is sustainable.
findings.quote: Model the financial impact of rent convergence from April 2027. This is Consumer Prices Index (CPI) +1% +£1 for 2027/28 and CPI+1%+£2 from 2028/29. Cabinet has approved the inclusion of rent convergence in budget setting proposals from 2027/28

findings.committee: Finance and Economic Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Appendix B for Housing Revenue Account Provisional Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: External consultants commissioned for critical friend review of 30-year HRA business plan due August 2026
findings.detail: The council has appointed external consultants to review the 30-year business plan, with the review commissioned for completion by August 2026. The council explicitly notes that assumptions built into the plan carry sensitivity and that variations can have significant financial impact.
findings.matters: External validation of a business plan suggests the council wanted independent assurance of its strategy; the sensitivity note indicates small changes in assumptions could materially affect affordability.
findings.figures: 30-year business plan; completion due August 2026
findings.quote: To review key assumptions built into business plan to ensure they are accurate. Due to the sensitivity of the assumptions, any variations can have significant impact

findings.committee: Finance and Economic Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Appendix B for Housing Revenue Account Provisional Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Council is prioritising tenant arrears collection with dedicated officer and software optimisation
findings.detail: A former tenant arrears officer has been put in post and is undertaking tracing of arrears using external agencies. Separately, the council is analysing specialist software providers to automate rent collection. The stated objective is improvement in collection rates and reduction in write-offs for bad debts.
findings.matters: The deployment of dedicated resources and software investment suggests arrears are material; debt write-offs and collection failures affect HRA cash flow and debt sustainability.
findings.figures: None specified in update
findings.quote: Former tenant arrears officer in post currently undertaking tracing, utilising external agencies. Undertaking analysis of software providers who specialise in optimum automation of rent collection

findings.committee: Finance and Economic Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Appendix B for Housing Revenue Account Provisional Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Council had significant budget variances in capital programme and is now implementing tighter virement controls
findings.detail: The council identified significant overspends in the HRA capital programme and has responded by putting budget virement controls in place. New procedures now require that orders can only be raised where budget availability exists, and no further overspends against individual schemes or preventative budget movements will be approved.
findings.matters: Lenders care about past capital control failures and whether they have been genuinely fixed; tight virement controls suggest the council learned from this.
findings.figures: significant budget variances in the capital programme
findings.quote: In response to significant budget variances in the capital programme, undertake regular budget virements to ensure orders can only be raised where there is budget availability

findings.headline: Pay inflation running ahead of budget assumptions
findings.detail: The council implemented a 3.2% pay award for 2025/26 compared to only 2% budgeted. While contained this year through maintaining a 3% vacancy factor, this shows pay inflation outpacing budget assumptions.
findings.matters: Sustained pay inflation beyond budget assumptions, even if managed through vacancies this year, creates structural pressure on future budgets that may be harder to absorb if vacancy rates cannot be maintained.
findings.figures: Pay award 3.2% vs 2% budgeted; salary outturn £58k overspend despite being £125k below budget.
findings.quote: A pay award in line with the national award for 2025/26 of 3.2% was implemented during the year. This award was higher than the 2% budgeted but it has been possible to contain the increase during the year and achieve the salary vacancy factor of 3%.

findings.headline: Council using revenue reserves to fund capital expenditure
findings.detail: The Local Priorities Reserve declined by £5.564m, with £2.136m transferred to provide a contribution to capital financing. This indicates the council is drawing down general reserves to fund capital work, suggesting capital funding pressure.
findings.matters: Using revenue reserves to finance capital reduces financial buffers and typically signals tight funding, weakening resilience to unexpected shocks.
findings.figures: Local Priorities Reserve: £5.564m net decrease; £2.136m used for capital financing contribution. Total Revenue Reserves: £22.992m (down from £26.626m opening balance).
findings.quote: £2.136m to provide a contribution for capital financing.

findings.headline: Council must fund an unquantified transition to Local Government Reorganisation
findings.detail: The council states it will be required to provide funding to transition to new Local Government Reorganisation arrangements, but no cost estimate or timeline is provided. The council will need to present a future financial proposal to cover these costs.
findings.matters: An unquantified future liability that will reduce financial flexibility and repayment headroom; the scale and timing are unknown pending government announcement.
findings.figures: No figures provided; timing and quantum still to be determined.
findings.quote: The Council must also prepare for the financial structural changes of Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) (although at the time of compiling this report no announcement has been made). Therefore, it will be necessary to present a future financial proposal as the Council will be required to provide funding in order to transition towards the new arrangements.

findings.headline: Business rate reset and deteriorating medium-term financial outlook
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies that the recent Local Government funding review's reset of the Business Rate system is 'not favourable towards district councils'. The council states that 'the medium-term financial outlook remains difficult', indicating anticipated income pressures ahead.
findings.matters: Structural erosion of business rate income directly affects the council's repayment capacity and financial sustainability over the lending horizon.
findings.figures: Business rates collected £45.295m of £45.874m debit (98.74%). Council ranks 34th nationally for collection, up from 54th.
findings.quote: This reset is not favourable towards district councils, and the medium-term financial outlook remains difficult.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Provisional Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Investment income fell £384k due to depleted reserve balances earning less return
findings.detail: Investment income was £384k below budget because average HRA reserve balances were lower than anticipated. Prior-year reserve draws and in-year funding draw-downs reduced the capital available to generate returns, creating a negative feedback loop where reserves are depleted faster.
findings.matters: Reduced income from reserves compounds financial stress. Depleted reserves earn less, requiring further draws to maintain operations, which further reduces income—a cycle that erodes financial flexibility and increases dependence on borrowing.
findings.figures: Investment income variance £384k adverse
findings.quote: reduced investment income returns of £384k due to the average balances across the HRA reserves being lower than anticipated with the draw on reserves as part of the outturn in 2024/25 then the additional funding drawn down in year.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Provisional Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Dwelling rental income fell £294k short of budget, with ongoing structural risk from Universal Credit migration
findings.detail: Actual dwelling rent income was £29.562m vs budget £29.856m—a £294k shortfall. Collection rates hit 97.30% vs 97.35% target. The council notes that Universal Credit migration has reduced direct payments to rent accounts; Housing Benefit previously went to the council, but UC recipients receive payments directly and may deprioritize rent payments.
findings.matters: Rental income funds HRA operations and debt service. UC migration is a structural shift that could worsen over time: if tenants receiving UC directly are more likely to underpay or default, collection rates could deteriorate further, pressuring reserves and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: Dwelling rents £29.562m vs budget £29.856m (£294k shortfall); collection rate 97.30% vs 97.35% target
findings.quote: Universal Credit migration has reduced direct payments to the rent account – previously, Housing Benefit would be paid direct to the rent account, however, for some of those tenants who have migrated to Universal Credit, their Housing Costs are paid direct to them.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Provisional Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Capital maintenance programme underperformed: only 2,049 of 2,340 planned component replacements completed (87%)
findings.detail: The council completed 291 fewer component replacements than targeted. Shortfalls occurred across kitchens (47 short), bathrooms (79 short), boilers (37 short), external refurbishments (119 short), and other workstreams. The council attributes this to durability checks delaying work, but it represents deferred maintenance that will accumulate.
findings.matters: Underperformance on maintenance targets creates a future liability spiral: deferred work ages the stock faster, requiring larger and costlier repairs later—the exact dynamic that caused this year's £2.7m crisis. This suggests the maintenance backlog is growing.
findings.figures: 2,049 actual vs 2,340 target (291 shortfall); kitchens 235 vs 282, bathrooms 179 vs 258, boilers 286 vs 323, external refurbishments 849 vs 968
findings.quote: A total of 2,049 component replacements or upgrades to Council homes were completed in year against a target of 2,340

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Provisional Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: HRA reserves depleted by £7.5m to cover in-year pressures, reducing total reserves from £35.7m to £28.2m
findings.detail: Total HRA reserves fell by £7.483m in a single year. The Reactive Repairs Reserve was fully exhausted (£1m to £0). HRA Priorities Reserve fell by £2.014m and Major Repairs Reserve by £4.957m. This depletion funded the increased repairs budget and other in-year costs, consuming financial buffers rather than building them.
findings.matters: Large single-year reserve draws indicate poor financial planning and erode the council's financial resilience. Combined with the in-year repairs crisis, it shows the HRA is using reserves to manage current pressures rather than investing in future improvements—a key solvency indicator.
findings.figures: Total HRA reserves £35.723m down to £28.240m; Reactive Repairs Reserve £1m to £0; HRA Priorities Reserve £5.761m to £3.747m; Major Repairs Reserve £15.316m to £10.359m
findings.quote: additional £1m to fund the remaining element of the revised increased revenue budget taken to Council in year to fund the increase in repairs and maintenance works.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Provisional Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Repairs and maintenance budget required an unplanned £2.7m increase mid-year
findings.detail: The council faced unexpected financial pressures during 2025/26 in repairs and maintenance. The original budget of £10.6m was increased in-year to £13.6m—a 28% increase—to fund necessary work. Actual spending reached £13.7m, indicating the council underestimated or encountered unforeseen maintenance liabilities in its housing stock.
findings.matters: For a lender, an unplanned 28% budget surge in a core service suggests either weak asset management visibility or deteriorating property condition. This signals the council may not have full control of its maintenance liabilities.
findings.figures: Original repairs budget £10.617m, increased to £13.6m in-year, actual outturn £13.681m (£96k over revised budget)
findings.quote: the HRA has faced financial challenges during the year specifically the repairs and maintenance budgets which required an additional £2.7m revenue budget increase in-year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025/26
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account viability sustainability review commissioned with September 2026 deadline
findings.detail: The council identifies HRA viability pressure as its 9th strategic risk, citing challenges in providing and maintaining quality social housing. The council has commissioned a formal Housing Revenue Account financials sustainability review and 30-year business plan, due September 2026, under the Deputy Chief Executive and Section 151 Officer.
findings.matters: A council undertaking a dedicated HRA sustainability review suggests concern about long-term viability of social housing provision, which could require increased general fund subsidy or reduction in service capacity.
findings.figures: HRA review deadline: September 2026; HRA identified as strategic risk #9
findings.quote: Increasing pressure on the Housing Revenue Account (HRA) viability due to the challenges of providing and maintaining quality social housing provision within the district.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025/26
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates fundamental structural uncertainty with decision expected July 2026
findings.detail: The council lists Local Government Reorganisation as its 10th strategic risk. The council submitted an LGR proposal to MHCLG in March 2025 and provided formal consultation response in November 2025. Seven workstreams are ongoing under a 'no regrets' work phase. A decision on LGR structure is expected July 2026, with district elections possibly scheduled for May 2027.
findings.matters: Fundamental uncertainty about whether the council will continue in its current form creates risk to lending arrangements, governance continuity, and long-term financial planning.
findings.figures: LGR decision expected July 2026; Elections possibly May 2027; 7 workstreams ongoing
findings.quote: The implications and general uncertainty of Local Government Reorganisation on the Council

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025/26
findings.headline: Stock Control audit at new Operations Depot received Limited assurance on both design and effectiveness
findings.detail: The internal audit of stock control at the council's new Operations Depot, which opened in December 2025, is the only audit to receive Limited assurance ratings on both design and effectiveness. This represents a specific control weakness in a newly operationalized facility. Management has acknowledged this was a known area of concern and states action has been taken to improve controls.
findings.matters: A Limited assurance rating on both design and effectiveness of controls indicates specific control failures in asset management that could affect financial accuracy and increases audit risk in a new operation.
findings.figures: 1 of 13 audits received Limited assurance; 11 assurance reviews undertaken in 2025/26
findings.quote: we would draw attention to the Stock Management review which was the only limited assurance audit this year. This was a known area of concern and action has been taken to improve controls in this area.

findings.headline: Payroll system (iTrent) has control gaps affecting payroll design, though operational effectiveness remains substantial
findings.detail: The audit found gaps within the iTrent payroll system controls that impact payroll control design. Despite these identified gaps, the audit concluded that operational effectiveness was substantial, meaning controls are being consistently applied despite the design weakness.
findings.matters: Payroll is typically one of the largest financial transactions and a fraud-risk area. Gaps in system controls, even if current operation is effective, create vulnerability to future errors or misuse, particularly if staffing changes occur.
findings.figures: Not quantified; Payroll audit gave Moderate design and Substantial operational effectiveness opinions; 2 medium, 0 low recommendations
findings.quote: Similarly, there are gaps within the iTrent system controls which impact payroll control design. However, the effectiveness was found to be substantial despite the potential gaps.

findings.headline: Lack of documented financial policies in key areas creating inconsistencies across Main Financial System, Stock Management, Voids, and Building Control
findings.detail: The audit identified that several critical areas lack documented, corporate-wide policies and procedures, resulting in inconsistencies in how controls are operated across the council. This was explicitly noted for Main Financial System controls, Voids Management, Stock Management, and Building Control.
findings.matters: Undocumented or inconsistently-applied financial controls increase the risk of errors, duplicate work, and failure to catch exceptions. This is particularly material in Main Financial System controls, the backbone of the council's financial reporting.
findings.figures: Four key areas identified with documentation gaps; 39 total recommendations issued (up from 28 in 2024/25)
findings.quote: In some areas there was a lack of documented policies and procedures which resulted in inconsistencies across the Council. Notably, this was the case in relation to Main Financial System controls, Voids Management, Stock Management and Building Control, where a lack of a single corporate policy weakened the control system.

findings.headline: Audit opinions deteriorated year-on-year, with positive ratings dropping from 100% to 91%
findings.detail: In 2024/25, all audit opinions were either substantial or moderate assurance. In 2025/26, 91% are substantial or moderate, meaning one limited assurance opinion has been introduced (Stock Management). Additionally, three high-risk recommendations were raised in 2025/26 compared to zero high-risk recommendations in 2024/25.
findings.matters: A deterioration in control opinion from one year to the next signals that the council's control environment has weakened. Moving from 100% to 91% positive ratings, plus the introduction of high-risk findings, indicates emerging control challenges that require management attention.
findings.figures: 2024/25: 100% substantial/moderate opinions, zero high recommendations. 2025/26: 91% substantial/moderate opinions, 3 high recommendations
findings.quote: The total proportion of positive design (substantial and moderate) opinions has dropped from the prior year from 100% to 91%. In 2024/25 there was two substantial and five moderate control design opinions issued to the Council. In comparison in 2025/26, there has been five substantial, five moderate design, but one limited opinion issued to the Council.

findings.headline: Unit4 financial system recently implemented but still embedding with acknowledged access control gaps
findings.detail: The council deployed a new workflow-driven financial system (Unit4) with embedded approval routes. The audit found that these processes are still being embedded and refined, and there is explicit scope to improve user access controls, though the review did not identify evidence of actual malpractice.
findings.matters: A newly-implemented core financial system with acknowledged access control gaps poses a control risk. Until the system and controls are fully embedded and access properly restricted, the council operates with a weakened financial control environment during a critical transition.
findings.figures: Not quantified; relates to Financial Systems and General Ledger audit which gave Moderate design and Substantial operational effectiveness opinions
findings.quote: The Council has recently implemented a workflow-driven financial system (Unit4) with embedded approval routes, the processes of which however are still being embedded and refined. There is scope to further improve user access controls, although our reviews did not identify any evidence of malpractice.

findings.headline: Stock Management received limited assurance, the council's only control weakness at that level this year
findings.detail: Stock Management is the only area where the internal audit gave a limited assurance opinion on both control design and operational effectiveness. It carried three high-risk recommendations—the first time any audit in the council received high-risk findings. The audit team notes this was a known area of concern and that action has been taken to address it.
findings.matters: Limited assurance means the system of internal controls is weakened and objectives are at risk. High-risk recommendations indicate substantial risk of loss, fraud, impropriety, or failure to achieve objectives. These are material control failures in an operational area.
findings.figures: 3 high, 9 medium, 3 low recommendations in Stock Management; zero high recommendations in prior year (2024/25)
findings.quote: No audits received no assurance ratings although we would draw attention to the Stock Management review which was the only limited assurance audit this year. This was a known area of concern and action has been taken to improve controls in this area.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - General Fund Finance Risk Register 2026-27
findings.headline: Asset maintenance backlog persists with medium-term outlook of sustained high expenditure
findings.detail: The council has allocated additional funding in 2026/27 to address backlog maintenance of council assets and is reviewing capacity for large-scale property projects. The risk register explicitly states the medium-term outlook shows continuation of high maintenance levels that will require ongoing financing.
findings.matters: Sustained high maintenance expenditure indicates deferred asset renewal, constrains financial flexibility to manage other pressures, and may indicate aging asset base requiring capital renewal.
findings.figures: Additional funding included in 2026/27 budget (amount not specified); described as "high levels of maintenance"
findings.quote: The medium-term outlook is a continuation of high levels of maintenance that will require financing.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - General Fund Finance Risk Register 2026-27
findings.headline: Capital borrowing identified as medium-term risk, currently avoidable but under active review
findings.detail: The council rates capital borrowing as a high-risk prospect (score 12). While the capital programme is currently financed without borrowing, this position is explicitly "kept under review". The council plans financial modelling to assess borrowing consequences and alignment with required savings before any decision is made.
findings.matters: Future capital borrowing by a council forecasting structural deficits from 2027/28 compounds financial pressure and constrains flexibility; it signals capital needs may coincide with revenue stress.
findings.figures: Likelihood 3, Impact 3, residual risk score 12 rated High
findings.quote: The capital programme can currently be financed without borrowing although this is kept under review.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - General Fund Finance Risk Register 2026-27
findings.headline: Government funding settlement has reduced, with deficits forecast from 2027/28 onwards
findings.detail: The government's multi-year funding review resulted in reduced funding from 2026/27. A one-off grant provides relief in 2026/27 only, but overall funding will reduce over the three-year settlement period. The council explicitly forecasts deficits beginning in 2027/28 and notes it must manage reductions to achieve balance from that point forward.
findings.matters: A structural funding deficit indicates the council will need to find significant savings, draw down reserves, or increase income — each has implications for repayment capacity and financial sustainability that directly interest lenders.
findings.figures: Deficits forecast from 2027/28; three-year settlement period; one-off grant for 2026/27 only
findings.quote: Overall funding amounts will reduce over the three-year period and despite the transitional funding arrangements deficits are forecast from 2027/28.

findings.headline: Investment income declining from 4.50% to 3.00% as rates fall; headwind to budget
findings.detail: Budgeted investment earnings are forecast to fall from 4.50% (2025/26) to 3.50% (2026/27) to 3.00% (2028/29), reflecting expected Bank Rate reductions from 3.75% to 3.25%. On projected investment balances of £46.329m (2026/27), this decline represents approximately £600k lower annual investment income by 2028/29.
findings.matters: Investment returns are a material income source for councils. The 150 basis-point decline in budgeted yields over three years reduces financial headroom for reserves and general spending. This creates pressure on the revenue budget as interest rates fall.
findings.figures: Budgeted investment returns declining from 4.50% (2025/26) to 3.00% (2028/29); expected investment balances 2026/27: £46.329m
findings.quote: The suggested budgeted investment earnings rates for returns on investments placed for periods up to about three months during each financial year are as follows (the long-term forecast is for periods over 10 years in the future): 2025/26 3.80% 4.50%; 2026/27 3.40% 3.50%; 2027/28 3.30% 3.25%; 2028/29 3.30% 3.00%

findings.headline: Under-borrowing strategy of £41m is entirely dependent on interest rates falling as forecast
findings.detail: The council maintains a Capital Financing Requirement of £104.323m but holds only £66.881m external debt (2026/27), creating a £41.276m under-borrowed position. Section 3.15 justifies this: 'This strategy is prudent as medium and longer dated borrowing rates are expected to fall from their current levels.' However, section 3.17 flags contingency: if rates rise sharply instead, 'fixed rate funding will be drawn whilst interest rates are lower than they are projected to be in the next few years.'
findings.matters: Interest rate forecasts are subject to significant error. If MUFG's forecast of falling rates proves wrong and rates instead rise, the council's decision to defer £41m of borrowing could prove expensive, forcing future borrowing at higher rates than currently anticipated. This represents material budget risk.
findings.figures: CFR 2026/27: £104.323m; external debt: £66.881m; under-borrowing: £41.276m. Forecast PWLB 5-year rates: Mar 2026 4.60%, declining to Dec 2027 4.10%
findings.quote: The Council is currently maintaining an under-borrowed position. This means that the capital borrowing need, (the Capital Financing Requirement), has not been fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the Authority's reserves, balances and cash flow has been used as a temporary measure. This strategy is prudent as medium and longer dated borrowing rates are expected to fall from their current levels

findings.headline: Capital receipts of £13.3m are essential to avoid borrowing in 2026/27
findings.detail: The 2026/27 capital programme of £30.756m is financed by capital receipts (£13.300m), grants (£3.475m), and reserves (£13.981m), with zero net new borrowing needed. Capital receipts represent 43% of required financing. These are one-off asset sales; if forecast sales underperform, the council must either borrow or cut the capital programme.
findings.matters: Reliance on one-off capital receipts creates vulnerability. Asset sales are unpredictable and unsustainable as an ongoing funding source. If property disposals fail to deliver, the council faces forced borrowing at potentially higher rates or capital programme cuts with service consequences.
findings.figures: 2026/27 capital receipts: £13.300m of £30.756m total capital expenditure (43%)
findings.quote: Financing of capital expenditure 2026/27: Capital receipts reserve 13.300

findings.headline: Capital expenditure plan dropping 47% in one year, from £30.8m to £16.2m
findings.detail: Capital expenditure falls from £39.735m (2025/26) to £30.756m (2026/27), then drops sharply to £16.191m (2027/28)—a 47% reduction. Spending then remains flat at £15.9m through 2028/29. This decline is driven by reduced HRA capital investment (from £21.414m down to £13.110m in 2027/28).
findings.matters: Sharp reductions in capital investment signal either strategic retrenchment or financial constraint. For lenders, this indicates reduced investment in asset maintenance and infrastructure. For finance directors, declining investment plans suggest pressure on capital resources or a shift away from renewal activity.
findings.quote: Capital Expenditure Total 36.550 39.735 30.756 16.191 15.996

findings.headline: Major Repairs Reserve halving to £2.5m from £10.5m over three years
findings.detail: The Major Repairs Reserve (which funds routine HRA maintenance) is forecast to decline from £10.508m in 2025/26 to £4.985m in 2026/27, and to £2.529m by 2027/28—a 76% reduction over three years. Given the HRA annual revenue of £32.304m (2026/27), a reserve of £2.5m represents only 0.94 months of revenue, reducing the council's maintenance flexibility.
findings.matters: Lower maintenance reserves force shift toward reactive rather than preventive maintenance, increasing long-term asset deterioration risk, tenant complaints, and compliance issues. Lenders and finance directors assess housing quality through maintenance spend and reserve adequacy.
findings.quote: Major Repairs Reserve    15.316    10.508    4.985    2.529    2.796

findings.headline: HRA capital reserves collapsing from £12m to near-zero in three years
findings.detail: The HRA's capital reserves are forecast to decline from £12.038m in 2025/26 to £2.416m in 2026/27, and to £0.285m by 2028/29. This represents an 80% reduction in one year, with reserves essentially exhausted by the end of the forecast period. These reserves provide essential buffers for the council's 5,846 HRA dwellings.
findings.matters: For an HRA holding nearly 5,850 dwellings, capital reserves provide buffers for urgent repairs and unexpected asset failures. Depleting these to near-zero creates material risk of deferred maintenance and severely limits the council's ability to respond to emergencies or reactive demand.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - HRA Finance Risk Register 2026-27
findings.headline: Collection of former tenant arrears continues as ongoing challenge; economic pressures increasing bad debt risk
findings.detail: The register identifies increased bad debts from economic circumstances as a risk to HRA income (score 8). Rent collection is the key income source for the HRA. Former tenant arrears collection remains a challenge and the council is exploring alternative collection methods including outsourcing.
findings.matters: Rent arrears reduce HRA revenue and cash flow; economic deterioration could worsen collection rates at a time when reserves are already under pressure
findings.figures: Risk score 8
findings.quote: Collection of former tenant arrears continues to be a challenge and alternative collection methods including outsourcing is being explored.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - HRA Finance Risk Register 2026-27
findings.headline: 2026/27 budget includes mandated continued investment in housing stock to meet government decent homes requirements
findings.detail: Budget proposals for 2026/27 include continued significant spending on social housing stock to meet new government decent homes standard requirements (High risk, score 12). This adds to capital spending pressures already identified in reserve and affordability risks.
findings.matters: Mandated government spending requirements limit discretion in HRA planning and exacerbate affordability pressures
findings.figures: 2026/27, Risk score 12 (High)
findings.quote: The budget proposals for 2026/27 include continued significant in the social housing stock which is required to meet new government requirements for decent homes standard.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - HRA Finance Risk Register 2026-27
findings.headline: HRA Business Plan is structurally unbalanced between revenue repairs spending and capital programme requirements
findings.detail: The council identifies an unbalanced HRA Business Plan (High risk, score 14) where balancing increased revenue spending on repairs/maintenance and regulatory compliance against capital programme delivery is critical. Treasury advisors commissioned to review debt refinancing options.
findings.matters: Structural imbalance in the HRA model suggests affordability challenges that may require changes to rent setting or service levels
findings.figures: Risk score 14 (High)
findings.quote: The balance between increased revenue spend dealing with repairs and maintenance, regulatory compliance and ensuing decent homes against the delivery of with capital programme will be key.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - HRA Finance Risk Register 2026-27
findings.headline: Reserve balances depleting unsustainably over the next three years due to capital program financing
findings.detail: The risk register identifies significant reduction in reserve balances over the 3-year period due to capital program financing as unsustainable (High risk, score 14). A fundamental review using stock condition data is necessary to plan medium-term investment levels sustainably.
findings.matters: Depletion of reserves reduces financial flexibility and ability to manage unexpected pressures or economic downturns; critical for lender credit assessment
findings.figures: 3-year period, significant reduction in reserve balances
findings.quote: Over the next 3-year period as a consequence of future spending levels there is a significant reduction in reserve balances due to the financing of the capital program which is unstainable.

findings.headline: S151 Officer declares current HRA spending plans unsustainable; urgent review required
findings.detail: The s151 Officer has explicitly stated that HRA spending levels for 2026/27 onwards 'are not sustainable' and that an urgent review of the HRA Business Plan will be carried out. This is the finance officer's direct assessment of viability, not a routine comment.
findings.matters: The s151 Officer's explicit warning of unsustainability indicates the council recognises it cannot continue current spending patterns without major operational change, rent increases, or external support.
findings.figures: none
findings.quote: the financial proposals for 2026/27 onwards show further reserve reductions based on current spending plans for both capital and revenue and these expenditure levels are not sustainable. Consequently, an urgent review of the HRA Business Plan will be carried out to ensure the ongoing sustainability of the HRA

findings.headline: HRA showing forecast overspend in 2025/26 despite £2.8m emergency funding
findings.detail: The council approved one-off emergency funding of £2.781m in November 2025 to address HRA financial pressures, but the latest monitoring report for quarter 3 still shows a forecast overspend. This indicates underlying revenue pressures are larger than emergency funding can address.
findings.matters: Persistent overspending despite emergency intervention indicates structural, not cyclical, revenue problems that threaten the HRA's medium-term viability and suggest management's forecasting accuracy is poor.
findings.figures: £2.781m emergency funding; quarter 3 of 2025/26
findings.quote: In November 2025, the Council approved one-off funding of £2.781m for the financial year 2025/26. However, despite this increase, spending pressures remain with the latest monitoring report for 2025/26 (as at end of quarter 3) showing a forecast overspend.

findings.headline: HRA projected to fall into deficit by 2032/33 under current spending plans
findings.detail: The council's longer-term business plan projections show it will need to draw on further reserves and potentially enter deficit by 2032/33 unless corrective action is taken. This depends partly on adoption of rent convergence proposals, which remain uncertain.
findings.matters: An HRA deficit would signal the council cannot sustain its housing function from income and reserves, forcing either substantial rent increases, service cuts, or borrowing at a time when both options are politically and financially constrained.
findings.quote: longer-term projections show the need to draw on further reserves before potentially falling into a deficit by 2032/33

findings.headline: Major Repairs Reserve forecast to collapse from £15.3m to £2.1m by 2029
findings.detail: The Major Repairs Reserve will fall from £15.316m at March 2025 to only £2.063m by March 2029. Overall HRA reserves are forecast to reduce from £35.723m to £7.752m in the same period, driven by capital programme spending and revenue pressures continuing.
findings.matters: Depleting reserves mean the council has severely limited financial flexibility to respond to maintenance emergencies, capital shortfalls, or unexpected cost increases in its housing stock.
findings.figures: £15.316m (March 2025) to £2.063m (March 2029); overall reserves from £35.723m to £7.752m
findings.quote: the MRR balance is forecast to significantly decrease from £15.316m as at 31 March 2025 to a projected balance of £2.063m at 31 March 2029. Together with the increased pressure in dealing with the revenue repairs and maintenance issues which has continued throughout 2025/26, despite the increased in budget agreed in year, is putting a severe financial strain on the HRA. As a result, the overall level of reserves forecast to reduce from £35.723m at 31 March 2025 to £7.752m at 31 March 2029.

findings.headline: Total investment exposure forecast to decline 31% over three years—from £70.9m to £49.0m—with treasury investments falling 37%
findings.detail: The council projects total investment exposure declining from £70.913m (2025/26) to £48.976m (2027/28), a £21.9m reduction. Treasury management investments alone fall from £58.647m to £36.764m. The document confirms 'the council has currently funded all investments with usable reserves,' meaning this decline represents material depletion of liquid financial assets.
findings.matters: Reserve consumption of this magnitude—nearly a third in three years—signals the council's liquid financial cushion will be substantially eroded by 2027/28, reducing financial resilience and flexibility to respond to challenges.
findings.figures: Total investments: £70.913m (2025/26) → £48.976m (2027/28); Treasury management investments: £58.647m (2025/26) → £36.764m (2027/28)
findings.quote: The council has currently funded all investments with usable reserves.

findings.headline: Council explicitly states external borrowing is necessary because reserves are insufficient for its capital ambitions
findings.detail: The strategy states that 'borrowing funds from external sources is considered to be necessary given the available level of reserves available to fund the Council's capital ambitions.' This statement is made in the context of acknowledging a 'challenging financial landscape.' The council commits to 'careful financial modelling' to ensure any borrowing can be supported over the loan duration.
findings.matters: For lenders, this signals that the council's capital plans are now reserve-constrained and new external borrowing is required. The explicit acknowledgment of both insufficient reserves and a challenging financial context is a material indicator of financial pressure driving borrowing need.
findings.figures: Specific forward borrowing amounts are in Treasury Management Strategy; this document establishes the driver.
findings.quote: Borrowing funds from external sources is considered to be necessary given the available level of reserves available to fund the Council's capital ambitions. However, there is careful consideration of the financing implications of undertaking borrowing in the context of the Medium-Term Financial Plan and the challenging financial landscape.

findings.paper_title: Budget Proposals for 202627 and Indicative Budgets for 202728 and 202829 General Fund_v2
findings.headline: Asset sales exhausted; capital programme no longer self-financing from disposals
findings.detail: The council has relied for several years on selling surplus assets to fund its capital programme. It now reports that 'the identification of further assets for disposal is now limited' and states it will 'continue to be financed from internal resources until borrowing is the only available option'.
findings.matters: The council is approaching a point where it will need to borrow to fund capital investment, which increases its borrowing costs and debt service obligations. The current capital programme (2026/27 spend of £3.334m) is being covered by capital receipts and reserves, but this is not sustainable.
findings.figures: Capital programme 2026/27 £3.334m financed from capital receipts (£2.297m), grants (£0.998m), and reserves (£1.285m); capital reserves forecast to decline from £3.658m to £0.579m by 2029
findings.quote: the identification of further assets for disposal is now limited.  Consequently, the capital programme will continue to be financed from internal resources until borrowing is the only available option.

findings.paper_title: Budget Proposals for 202627 and Indicative Budgets for 202728 and 202829 General Fund_v2
findings.headline: Unfunded statutory food waste collection obligation; lack of government clarity on new burdens funding
findings.detail: The Fair Funding Assessment assumes funding for 'Simpler Recycling new burdens' and weekly food waste collection (an Environment Act 2021 requirement), but the government has not itemised or explicitly allocated funds for this. The s151 Officer warns this lack of clarity may mean the funding reduction is even greater than forecast.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council will have to find savings or service reductions to deliver a new statutory obligation, or whether it will face a compliance gap. This is unquantified financial risk.
findings.figures: No funding line identified; assessment suggests funding shortfall possible beyond the £1.495m already identified
findings.quote: The lack of clarity over the 'new burdens' funding for weekly food waste collection service suggests the decrease might be even greater.

findings.paper_title: Budget Proposals for 202627 and Indicative Budgets for 202728 and 202829 General Fund_v2
findings.headline: New Homes Bonus ended; Local Priorities Reserve (primary discretionary pot) will not be replenished
findings.detail: New Homes Bonus receipts have historically been the main source of funding for the Local Priorities Reserve, which finances one-off investments and capital schemes. The Fair Funding Review ends this grant stream, and the s151 Officer expects the reserve to fall from £2.3m to £1.2m by 2029 with no mechanism to rebuild it.
findings.matters: The council's ability to respond to unforeseen capital needs or strategic opportunities is being eroded. A shrinking discretionary reserve reduces agility and resilience.
findings.figures: Local Priorities Reserve balance forecast to reduce to £1.2m by March 2029
findings.quote: the primary contributor is no longer available and therefore the balance is forecast to reduce to a balance of £1.2m by March 2029.

findings.paper_title: Budget Proposals for 202627 and Indicative Budgets for 202728 and 202829 General Fund_v2
findings.headline: General Fund reserves declining by £5m over three years; discretionary reserves falling sharply
findings.detail: Total General Fund reserves fall from £25.091m (March 2026) to £20.092m (March 2029). Discretionary reserves (the flexible pot) decline from £12.059m to £8.310m. These are being drawn to finance the capital programme and to build the Budget Stabilisation Reserve for the forecast 2027/28 and 2028/29 deficits.
findings.matters: A lender assesses whether a council has a buffer for shocks. A £5m reduction over three years is significant; if the forecast deficits exceed expectations, the council will burn through reserves faster and exhaust flexibility.
findings.figures: Total General Fund reserves: £25.091m (2026) → £20.092m (2029), a reduction of £4.999m; Discretionary reserves: £12.059m (2026) → £8.310m (2029)
findings.quote: Over the 3 year financial period the level of reserves reduces by £4.999m based on the forecast balance as at 31 March 2026.

findings.paper_title: Budget Proposals for 202627 and Indicative Budgets for 202728 and 202829 General Fund_v2
findings.headline: Structural government funding falls £1.495m by 2028/29, driving forecast deficits
findings.detail: If Council Tax is held flat, government funding to the council reduces from £10.793m to £9.298m between 2026/27 and 2028/29. The council is currently balancing 2026/27 only by relying on Council Tax rises up to the 2.99% limit and is already forecasting deficits of £532k (2027/28) and £1.283m (2028/29).
findings.matters: The council cannot balance its budget in years 2-3 of the MTFP without either finding savings of this scale, pushing Council Tax to politically difficult levels, or drawing reserves. It signals a period of financial pressure.
findings.figures: Government funding £10.793m 2026/27, falls to £9.298m 2028/29 (£1.495m cut); projected deficits of £532k and £1.283k in Table 3, rows 'Projected (Surplus)/Deficit'
findings.quote: If Council Tax increases are ignored, the Council's funding from Government actually reduces from £10.793m to £9.298m in 2028/29 – a reduction of £1.495m.

findings.paper_title: Budget Proposals for 202627 and Indicative Budgets for 202728 and 202829 General Fund_v2
findings.headline: Government baseline reset removes £619k permanently; one-year support grant masks the structural cut
findings.detail: The final settlement contained a late correction to baseline funding, removing £619k from South Kesteven's allocation. An 'Adjustment Support Grant' of £619k replaces this for 2026/27 only, with no assurance beyond that year. The s151 Officer explicitly notes this is temporary and leaves the council £1.495m worse off by 2028/29 if it is not renewed.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether council finances rest on one-off grants, and whether the council has identified how it will close a £619k structural gap when the grant expires
findings.figures: £619k removed from baseline funding in final settlement; £619k 'Adjustment Support Grant' for 2026/27 only; CSP drops from modelled base of £20.592m to £19.997m by 2028/29
findings.quote: However, the Government has stated this is for one-year only at present.

findings.headline: £189k of year-end expenditure not accrued and remains uncorrected in the financial statements
findings.detail: KPMG identified £189k of expenditure from April 2025 relating to 2024/25 that was not accrued. This was not corrected by management. While immaterial in isolation (1.47% of surplus), it represents a breach of accruals accounting principle and suggests potential year-end cutoff quality issues.
findings.matters: Uncorrected accruals errors indicate potential weaknesses in the council's month-end close process and financial statement preparation quality. This matters to lenders assessing asset quality and true financial position.
findings.figures: £189k uncorrected expenditure misstatement; 1.47% of reported surplus
findings.quote: We have identified 1 item of expenditure recorded in April 2025 which relate to 2024/25 and were incorrectly not accrued for.

findings.headline: Audit delays and additional costs incurred due to insufficient evidence quality and staffing constraints
findings.detail: KPMG identified that council staffing constraints and the quality of evidence submitted for audit caused unnecessary delays and inefficiencies. The audit fee overruns totalled £8,627 for delays and evidence quality issues, on top of a base fee of £165,842. This pattern of resource constraints mirrors the explanation for the accounts deadline misses.
findings.matters: Finance team capacity constraints affect the timeliness and quality of financial reporting. A lender should understand that the council's finance function is under resource pressure, which could impact both interim and year-end financial controls.
findings.figures: Audit fee overruns £8,627 for delays and quality of evidence; base fee £165,842; prior year fee £150,979
findings.quote: We encountered various delays during the audit due to insufficient evidence being provided for sample selected for testing, as well as delays due to Council staffing constraints.

findings.headline: Draft statement of accounts has missed the regulatory deadline in both 2023/24 and 2024/25
findings.detail: The council failed to produce the draft financial statements by the required reporting deadline in both years. Management attributes this to financial system changeover and staffing constraints. The 2025/26 closedown will be the first using the new finance system with new team members. This is flagged as a Priority 1 control deficiency meaning it could prevent the council meeting system objectives.
findings.matters: Repeated deadline misses signal potential finance team capacity or capability issues. A lender needs to know whether the council can reliably produce auditable accounts on time, especially given upcoming system and staffing changes.
findings.figures: Missed deadline in 2023/24; missed deadline in 2024/25
findings.quote: In 2023/24 and 2024/25 the draft statement of accounts were not produced in accordance with the reporting deadline.

news_drafts.headline: AI governance framework not yet in place despite staff using external tools without approval
news_drafts.lead: Data breaches from unsanctioned external AI tool use could create legal liability and regulatory intervention; governance lag on a rapidly-emerging risk creates operational and reputational exposure

news_drafts.headline: HRA faces very high financial pressure from rising demand and new building standards
news_drafts.lead: The HRA is a core revenue stream and borrowing vehicle for councils; pressure here signals funding stress that could constrain capital capacity or affect council creditworthiness

news_drafts.headline: Financing cost ratios diverged materially from budget
news_drafts.lead: Significant treasury variances affect forecast accuracy and cash flow planning; the finance director would need to understand what drove such large divergences.
